battle.title: Exception Escape Room
battle.description: Race through try, catch and finally to find the way out.

questions.text: Which of these is a checked exception that the compiler forces you to handle or declare?
questions.explanation: IOException extends Exception but not RuntimeException, so it is checked. The other three are unchecked RuntimeExceptions, which you may handle but the compiler does not require it.

The division throws, so B is skipped and the matching catch prints C. finally always runs (D), and since the exception was handled the program continues with E. Dropping D forgets that finally runs after a catch.
The finally block runs before the method actually returns to its caller, so 'fin' prints first, then main prints the returned 1. Many expect the return to happen first.

questions.text: A program reads a config file that might be missing. If it is missing it should continue with defaults, and an opened file must always be closed. What is the best approach?
options: Catch Exception around all of main and ignore it
Declare main throws Exception and let the program crash
Check file.exists() once and never use try/catch
try-with-resources, catching FileNotFoundException to fall back to defaults
questions.answer: try-with-resources, catching FileNotFoundException to fall back to defaults
questions.explanation: try-with-resources closes the file automatically and a specific catch lets you recover only from the expected problem. Swallowing every Exception hides real bugs, and exists() alone can still race with the file disappearing.
The return value 2 is evaluated and saved before finally runs. Assigning x = 3 in finally changes the variable but not the value already being returned, so 3 is the tempting but wrong answer.

coding.title: Safe Calculator
coding.description: Read n expressions of the form 'a op b' where op is one of + - * / %. Print the integer result of each. If the operation divides or takes the remainder by zero print ERROR. If a or b is not a valid integer, or op is not one of the five operators, print INVALID. Integer division truncates toward zero.
coding.inputDescription: Line 1: n. Next n lines: three space-separated tokens a op b.
coding.outputDescription: n lines, each a result, ERROR or INVALID.
coding.constraints: 1 <= n <= 1000, valid numbers fit comfortably in int and results never overflow

debug.title: The Loop That Gave Up
debug.description: The program reads n tokens, adds up the ones that are valid integers and counts the ones that are not. It should print 'sum badCount'. After the first bad token it stops reading the rest. Input: n, then n tokens. Output: the sum and the number of invalid tokens.
hints: Try '4' then '1 x 3 4'. Is 3 and 4 added to the sum?
Look at where the try and catch sit relative to the for loop.
When an exception is thrown inside the loop and the catch is outside it, what happens to the remaining iterations?
Move the try/catch inside the loop body so each token is handled on its own and the loop continues.
